chapter: Ch 15 — The Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999

questions.stem: Which of the following best states the objects of the Foreign Exchange Management Act 1999 as set out in its preamble?

readLink.label: Read: From FERA to FEMA — the shift and the objectives →

options.text: To conserve the foreign exchange resources of the country and to prevent their diversion to non-essential purposes
options.explanation: That is the FERA 1973 policy, framed for a country short of reserves. FEMA was enacted precisely to replace that conservation premise.

options.text: To facilitate external trade and payments, and to promote the orderly development and maintenance of the foreign exchange market in India
options.explanation: Correct. Both objects in the preamble are positive and facilitative — facilitation of external trade and payments, and an orderly foreign exchange market. Nothing in the preamble speaks of conservation or prevention.

options.text: To prohibit all dealings in foreign exchange except those specifically permitted by the Central Government
options.explanation: That inverts the Act. Under s. 5 a current account transaction is free unless restricted; only capital account transactions follow a permissible-classes approach.

options.text: To consolidate the law relating to foreign investment and to regulate the acquisition of Indian companies by non-residents
options.explanation: Foreign investment regulation is one consequence of s. 6, not the stated object of the Act, and takeovers of Indian companies are governed elsewhere.

questions.topic: Ch 15 · FERA to FEMA · Nature of a breach
questions.stem: Which statement most accurately describes the treatment of a breach under FEMA 1999 as compared with FERA 1973?
questions.sourceRef: FEMA 1999, ss. 13 and 14; contrast with FERA 1973

readLink.label: Read: From FERA to FEMA — the shift and the objectives →

options.text: Under FEMA every contravention remains a criminal offence, but the maximum term of imprisonment has been reduced
options.explanation: FEMA converted contraventions into civil wrongs. Imprisonment is not the ordinary consequence of a contravention at all.

options.text: Under FEMA a contravention is a civil wrong and imprisonment can never follow in any circumstances
options.explanation: Too absolute. Section 14 provides for civil imprisonment on failure to pay the penalty within 90 days of the notice of demand, and s. 13(1C) carries imprisonment in the aggravated s. 37A cases.

options.text: Under FEMA a contravention is a civil wrong attracting a monetary penalty on adjudication, imprisonment arising only on failure to pay the penalty and in the aggravated cases the Act specifies
options.explanation: Correct. Section 13 imposes a monetary penalty on adjudication; s. 14 attaches civil imprisonment to non-payment within 90 days of service of the demand notice; ss. 13(1A) to (1D) with s. 37A carry a separate criminal limb.

options.text: Under FEMA the burden of proving innocence continues to lie on the person proceeded against, as it did under FERA
options.explanation: The reverse onus was a FERA feature and was not carried into FEMA. Section 39 raises only a rebuttable presumption about documents, which is a different thing.

questions.stem: Section 1(2) of FEMA 1999 states the extent of the Act. The Act applies to:

readLink.label: Read: Extent and application — section 1 →

options.text: The whole of India; all branches, offices and agencies outside India owned or controlled by a person resident in India; and any contravention thereunder committed outside India by any person to whom the Act applies
options.explanation: Correct. These are the three limbs of s. 1(2), in order. Limb two reaches the entity abroad; limb three reaches the person wherever he commits the contravention.

options.text: The whole of India only, contraventions committed outside India being outside its reach
options.explanation: This drops limbs two and three. A contravention committed abroad by a person to whom the Act applies is expressly covered.

options.text: The whole of India and all branches, offices and agencies outside India of any Indian entity, whoever owns or controls them
options.explanation: The statutory test is ownership or control by a person resident in India, not merely that the entity is Indian in some looser sense; and this option still omits limb three.

options.text: The whole of India except the State of Jammu and Kashmir, together with branches abroad
options.explanation: FEMA carries no territorial exclusion of any State. The option imports a savings clause that does not exist.

questions.stem: For the purposes of section 2(v) of FEMA 1999, the basic day-count test for a person resident in India is residence in India for:

readLink.label: Read: Person resident in India — the section 2 residence test →

options.text: 182 days or more during the current financial year
options.explanation: Two errors. The threshold is 'more than' 182 days, so 182 exactly is not enough; and the year examined is the preceding financial year, not the current one.

options.text: More than 182 days during the current financial year
options.explanation: The threshold is right but the year is wrong. Status for a financial year is fixed by presence in the year before it.

options.text: 182 days or more during the preceding financial year
options.explanation: The year is right but the threshold is wrong. 'More than one hundred and eighty-two days' means 183 days at least.

options.text: More than 182 days during the preceding financial year
options.explanation: Correct. Section 2(v)(i) speaks of a person residing in India for more than 182 days during the course of the preceding financial year — that is, 183 days or more in the year 1 April to 31 March immediately before.

questions.stem: Mr Harold Pinto, a foreign national, arrives in India on 1 May 2025 to be with his daughter during her illness and stays continuously until 20 March 2026, taking no employment and carrying on no business here. For the financial year 2026-27 his status under FEMA is:

readLink.label: Read: Person resident in India — the section 2 residence test →

options.text: A person resident outside India, because he came to India otherwise than for employment, business or vocation, or for a stay of uncertain duration
options.explanation: Correct. Limb (B) of the carve-out in s. 2(v)(i) excludes a person who comes to or stays in India for any purpose other than employment, business or vocation, or an uncertain-period stay. The carve-out overrides the day count, so his 324 days are irrelevant.

options.text: A person resident in India, because he was physically present for more than 182 days in the preceding financial year
options.explanation: This applies the day count without reading the carve-out. The purpose test comes first and, once limb (B) is satisfied, the arithmetic never engages.

options.text: A person resident in India, because the length of his stay shows an intention to stay for an uncertain period
options.explanation: His purpose was defined and temporary — to be with his daughter during a specific illness. An uncertain-period stay is one where the circumstances indicate no fixed end, which is not the case on these facts.

options.text: A person resident outside India only until he completes 182 days, and a person resident in India thereafter
options.explanation: There is no mid-year switch. Status is determined by purpose first and then by the preceding financial year's day count, not by a running total in the current year.

questions.topic: Ch 15 · s. 2(v) · Offices, branches and agencies
questions.stem: Under FEMA 1999, which of the following is a 'person resident in India'?

readLink.label: Read: Person resident in India — the section 2 residence test →

options.text: Only an office or branch in India owned or controlled by a person resident outside India
options.explanation: Incomplete. That is one of the two limbs; the other — an office or branch outside India owned or controlled by a person resident in India — is equally a person resident in India.

options.text: Both an office, branch or agency in India owned or controlled by a person resident outside India, and an office, branch or agency outside India owned or controlled by a person resident in India
options.explanation: Correct. Section 2(v) reaches in both directions, which is why the Dubai branch of a Mumbai company and the Mumbai branch of a Dubai company are each a person resident in India.

options.text: Only an office or branch outside India owned or controlled by a person resident in India
options.explanation: Again only half the definition; the office in India owned or controlled by a non-resident is also caught.

options.text: Neither, because an office or branch is not a 'person' at all under section 2(u)
options.explanation: Section 2(u) expressly includes any agency, office or branch owned or controlled by a person within the definition of 'person'.

questions.topic: Ch 15 · s. 2(v) · Day count for the preceding financial year
questions.stem: Mr Kabir Shah was in India from 1 April 2025 to 15 July 2025 and again from 1 January 2026 to 31 March 2026, both dates inclusive, and was abroad on holiday for the rest of the year. He took no employment abroad and carried on no business abroad. For deciding his status for the financial year 2026-27, the number of days he resided in India during the preceding financial year is:
questions.sourceRef: FEMA 1999, s. 2(v)(i) — day count for the preceding financial year

readLink.label: Read: Person resident in India — the section 2 residence test →

options.text: 106 days, so he is a person resident outside India
options.explanation: 106 is only the first spell (1 April to 15 July 2025). The second spell of 90 days must be added; the test looks at total residence during the year, not at a single continuous stay.

options.text: 190 days, so he is a person resident in India
options.explanation: This is what you get by counting one of the spells exclusive of its end date. Both spells are inclusive of the first and last day, giving 106 and 90.

options.text: 196 days, so he is a person resident in India
options.explanation: Correct. 1 April to 15 July 2025 is 30 + 31 + 30 + 15 = 106 days; 1 January to 31 March 2026 is 31 + 28 + 31 = 90 days; total 196. That exceeds 182 and no carve-out applies, so he is a person resident in India for FY 2026-27.

options.text: 286 days, so he is a person resident in India
options.explanation: 286 counts the whole of April to July as four full months plus the January to March spell. July contributes only 15 days on these facts.

questions.stem: Ms Aarohi Nambiar was in India only from 1 June 2025 to 30 November 2025, both days inclusive, during the financial year 2025-26, and was outside India for the rest of that year purely on leisure travel. The number of days she resided in India during that financial year, and the consequence for the financial year 2026-27, are:
questions.sourceRef: FEMA 1999, s. 2(v)(i) — 'more than one hundred and eighty-two days'

readLink.label: Read: Person resident in India — the section 2 residence test →

options.text: 182 days; she is not a person resident in India, the threshold not being crossed
options.explanation: The arithmetic is wrong. June 30 + July 31 + August 31 + September 30 + October 31 + November 30 comes to 183, not 182.

options.text: 183 days; she is a person resident in India, having crossed the threshold by one day
options.explanation: Correct. 30 + 31 + 31 + 30 + 31 + 30 = 183. Because 'more than 182' means 183 or more, she clears the gate by exactly one day and, no carve-out applying, is a person resident in India for FY 2026-27.

options.text: 180 days; she is not a person resident in India
options.explanation: 180 treats the six months as six thirty-day months. Four of the six months in this spell have 31 days.

options.text: 184 days; she is a person resident in India
options.explanation: 184 double-counts a day at one end of the spell. Counting both 1 June and 30 November gives 183.

questions.stem: 'Repatriate to India' under section 2(y) of FEMA 1999 means:

readLink.label: Read: Person resident in India — the section 2 residence test →

options.text: Bringing into India the realised foreign exchange and selling it to an authorised person in exchange for rupees, or holding it in an account with an authorised dealer to the extent notified — and includes using the realised amount to discharge a debt owed outside India by a person resident in India
options.explanation: Correct. The definition has a conversion or parking limb and an express inclusion for the discharge of a debt owed outside India by a resident.

options.text: Merely bringing the foreign exchange physically into India, whatever is done with it afterwards
options.explanation: Bringing it in is not enough. It must be sold to an authorised person or held in a permitted authorised-dealer account; the channel is part of the definition.

options.text: Converting the foreign exchange into rupees anywhere in the world and remitting the rupee proceeds to India
options.explanation: Conversion must be effected by sale to an authorised person in India. A conversion abroad through some other channel is not repatriation.

options.text: Depositing the foreign exchange in any bank account outside India maintained by a person resident in India
options.explanation: That is the opposite of repatriation. Holding abroad is what ss. 4 and 8 restrict; the inclusion in s. 2(y) is confined to discharging a debt owed outside India.

questions.stem: Section 2(e) of FEMA 1999 defines a 'capital account transaction' as a transaction which:

readLink.label: Read: Capital account and current account transactions →

options.text: Involves the purchase or sale of a capital asset situated anywhere in the world by any person
options.explanation: The definition is not about capital assets as an accounting category. It turns on the alteration of cross-border assets or liabilities of a specified class of person.

options.text: Alters the assets or liabilities outside India of persons resident in India, or the assets or liabilities in India of persons resident outside India, and includes the transactions referred to in section 6(3)
options.explanation: Correct. The definition has two symmetrical limbs — the resident's position outside India and the non-resident's position in India — plus the inclusion of the s. 6(3) classes.

options.text: Alters the assets or liabilities in India of persons resident in India
options.explanation: That is a purely domestic alteration and is outside FEMA altogether. The definition is concerned only with cross-border positions.

options.text: Requires the prior approval of the Reserve Bank of India in every case, whatever its nature
options.explanation: This states a consequence, and states it too widely. Section 6 works by specifying permissible classes and limits; not every capital account transaction needs case-by-case approval.

questions.stem: Rahul, a person resident in India, remits USD 15,000 to a friend settled in Canada as a wedding gift. The remittance is not one of the four groups expressly listed in section 2(j). It is therefore:

readLink.label: Read: Capital account and current account transactions →

options.text: A capital account transaction, because it does not fall within any of the four groups listed in section 2(j)
options.explanation: This is the classic misreading. The four groups are illustrations introduced by 'without prejudice to the generality of the foregoing'; they do not exhaust the definition.

options.text: Neither a capital nor a current account transaction, and therefore outside FEMA
options.explanation: FEMA recognises only two classes of transaction. There is no third residual category outside the Act.

options.text: A current account transaction, because it is not a capital account transaction within section 2(e)
options.explanation: Correct. A gift leaves no one owning an asset or owing a liability across the border, so s. 2(e) is not satisfied and the transaction falls into the residual definition in s. 2(j). It is then restricted only by the Schedule III limit.

options.text: A capital account transaction, because a gift permanently transfers value out of India
options.explanation: Permanent loss of value is not the test. The test is whether cross-border assets or liabilities are altered, and a gift alters neither for either party.

questions.topic: Ch 15 · ss. 2(e) and 2(j) · Interest and principal
questions.stem: An Indian company has an external commercial borrowing from a lender abroad. It pays a quarterly interest instalment and, on maturity, repays the principal. Under FEMA these two payments are respectively:

readLink.label: Read: Capital account and current account transactions →

options.text: Both current account transactions
options.explanation: Only the interest is current. Repaying the principal extinguishes a liability outside India of a person resident in India, which is squarely within s. 2(e).

options.text: Both capital account transactions
options.explanation: Interest on loans is expressly named as a current account transaction in s. 2(j)(ii), so the two payments cannot be treated alike.

options.text: A capital account transaction and a current account transaction
options.explanation: The classification is the right way round for the two items but has been assigned to the wrong payment. Interest is current; principal is capital.

options.text: A current account transaction and a capital account transaction
options.explanation: Correct. Interest on loans is expressly a current account transaction under s. 2(j)(ii); repayment of principal alters a liability outside India and is a capital account transaction under s. 2(e). One loan therefore produces both kinds of transaction.

questions.stem: A demand draft is drawn in Chennai. Its amount is expressed in Indian rupees but it is payable, by its terms, in United States dollars. Under section 2(n) of FEMA 1999 the draft:

readLink.label: Read: Authorised persons and other key definitions →

options.text: Is foreign exchange, because the definition expressly covers drafts expressed in Indian currency but payable in foreign currency
options.explanation: Correct. Section 2(n) covers deposits, credits and balances payable in any foreign currency, and drafts, travellers' cheques, letters of credit and bills of exchange expressed or drawn in Indian currency but payable in any foreign currency. The currency of payment governs.

options.text: Is not foreign exchange, because it is expressed in Indian rupees
options.explanation: The currency of expression is not the test. The definition was drafted precisely to catch instruments expressed in rupees but payable abroad in foreign currency.

options.text: Is foreign exchange only if it is actually presented for payment outside India
options.explanation: The character of the instrument is fixed by its terms, not by where it is eventually presented.

options.text: Is a foreign security under section 2(o), not foreign exchange
options.explanation: A draft is not a security at all; s. 2(za) excludes bills of exchange and promissory notes other than Government promissory notes from the definition of security.

questions.stem: 'Authorised person' under section 2(c) of FEMA 1999 means:

readLink.label: Read: Authorised persons and other key definitions →

options.text: Any scheduled commercial bank in India
options.explanation: Neither necessary nor sufficient. A full-fledged money changer is not a bank, and a bank without an RBI authorisation under s. 10(1) is not an authorised person.

options.text: An authorised dealer, money changer, off-shore banking unit or any other person for the time being authorised under section 10(1) to deal in foreign exchange or foreign securities
options.explanation: Correct. These are the four limbs of s. 2(c). The status comes from the RBI's authorisation under s. 10(1), not from the entity's general character.

options.text: Any person permitted by the Central Government to hold foreign exchange
options.explanation: The authorising authority under s. 10(1) is the Reserve Bank, not the Central Government, and permission to hold is not the same as authorisation to deal.

options.text: Any person resident in India who has been allotted a limit under the Liberalised Remittance Scheme
options.explanation: An LRS remitter is a customer of an authorised person, not an authorised person. The LRS is a limit on drawal, not an authorisation to deal.

questions.stem: The Explanation to section 3(c) of FEMA 1999 provides that where a person receives in India a payment from, or by order or on behalf of, a person resident outside India without a corresponding inward remittance from outside India, he:
questions.sourceRef: FEMA 1999, s. 3(c) and the Explanation thereto

readLink.label: Read: Dealing in and holding foreign exchange — ss. 3 and 4 →

options.text: Is deemed to have received the payment through an authorised person, and no contravention arises
options.explanation: The Explanation works the other way. It deems the receipt to be outside the authorised channel, which is what makes it a contravention.

options.text: Must report the receipt to the Reserve Bank within thirty days, failing which it is treated as a contravention
options.explanation: No such reporting window exists in s. 3. The Explanation creates a deeming provision, not a reporting obligation with a cure period.

options.text: Shall be deemed to have received the payment otherwise than through an authorised person
options.explanation: Correct. The absence of a matching inward remittance is the marker of a parallel arrangement, and the Explanation deems the receipt to fall outside the authorised channel, bringing it within the s. 3(c) prohibition.

options.text: Is deemed to have made a capital account transaction requiring the prior approval of the Reserve Bank
options.explanation: The Explanation says nothing about classification. It addresses the channel of the receipt, and the transaction's character as current or capital is decided separately under ss. 2(e) and 2(j).

questions.stem: Meera, a person resident in India, wishes to gift USD 20,000 to her brother in Dubai — a purpose for which a remittance within the applicable limit is permissible. Instead of using her bank she pays the rupee equivalent in cash to an intermediary in Chennai, whose associate abroad credits the dollars to her brother's account. No money crosses the border. Which statement is correct?

readLink.label: Read: Dealing in and holding foreign exchange — ss. 3 and 4 →

options.text: There is no contravention, because the purpose of the remittance was itself permissible and the amount was within the limit
options.explanation: Section 3 is not concerned with the purpose. A permissible purpose sent outside the authorised channel is still a contravention.

options.text: There is no contravention, because no foreign exchange was bought or sold by Meera in India
options.explanation: Section 3(b) prohibits making any payment to or for the credit of a person resident outside India otherwise than as provided, whether or not Meera herself handled foreign currency.

options.text: There is a contravention only by the intermediary, Meera having merely paid rupees in India
options.explanation: Meera made the payment for the credit of a person resident outside India and dealt with a person other than an authorised person. She is a contravener in her own right.

options.text: There is a contravention of section 3, because the transaction bypassed an authorised person, and the penalty under section 13 runs on the whole sum involved
options.explanation: Correct. Clauses (a), (b) and (c) of s. 3 are each engaged, the Explanation to (c) deeming the receipt to be outside the authorised channel. The penalty base under s. 13(1) is the sum involved, not any profit made.

questions.topic: Ch 15 · s. 4 · Holding by a resident
questions.stem: Section 4 of FEMA 1999 provides that, save as otherwise provided in the Act, no person resident in India shall:

readLink.label: Read: Dealing in and holding foreign exchange — ss. 3 and 4 →

options.text: Acquire, hold, own, possess or transfer any foreign exchange, foreign security or immovable property situated outside India
options.explanation: Correct. Section 4 covers five verbs and three subject matters, and immovable property outside India is expressly one of them. The exceptions sit in ss. 6(4), 9 and the regulations.

options.text: Acquire or transfer any foreign exchange, mere holding or possession being outside the section
options.explanation: Holding, owning and possessing are each named in the section; the prohibition is not confined to acquisition and transfer.

options.text: Hold any foreign exchange or foreign security, immovable property outside India being governed only by section 6
options.explanation: Immovable property situated outside India appears in s. 4 itself. Section 6(4) then carves out property acquired while the person was resident outside India.

options.text: Hold any foreign exchange exceeding the equivalent of USD 2,50,000 at any time
options.explanation: There is no such threshold in s. 4. The USD 2,50,000 figure is the Liberalised Remittance Scheme ceiling on drawal in a financial year, an entirely different concept.

questions.topic: Ch 15 · s. 5 · Who may restrict a current account transaction
questions.stem: Under the proviso to section 5 of FEMA 1999, reasonable restrictions on current account transactions may be imposed by:

readLink.label: Read: Current account transactions — s. 5 and the Rules of 2000 →

options.text: The Reserve Bank, by regulations, in consultation with the Central Government
options.explanation: The authorities are the wrong way round for s. 5. Regulations made by the RBI belong to the capital account side under s. 6.

options.text: The Central Government, by rules, in the public interest and in consultation with the Reserve Bank
options.explanation: Correct. The proviso to s. 5 empowers the Central Government to impose reasonable restrictions by rules, in the public interest and in consultation with the Reserve Bank — which is why the Current Account Transactions Rules 2000 are Government rules.

options.text: The Reserve Bank alone, by directions issued to authorised persons
options.explanation: Directions under s. 11 bind authorised persons in their dealings; they are not the source of the restrictions on current account transactions listed in the three Schedules.

options.text: The Central Government alone, without any consultation, by notification
options.explanation: Consultation with the Reserve Bank is written into the proviso, as is the public-interest requirement. Both are conditions on the power.

questions.topic: Ch 15 · Current Account Rules · Schedule I
questions.stem: A resident individual applies to remit her winnings from a foreign lottery to a relative abroad. Under the Foreign Exchange Management (Current Account Transactions) Rules 2000 the correct position is:
questions.sourceRef: Current Account Transactions Rules 2000, Schedule I (rules-level)

readLink.label: Read: Current account transactions — s. 5 and the Rules of 2000 →

options.text: The remittance is free up to the Liberalised Remittance Scheme ceiling, and needs approval only beyond it
options.explanation: That is the Schedule III treatment. Remittance of lottery winnings is not a Schedule III item at all.

options.text: The remittance may be made with the prior approval of the Central Government department concerned
options.explanation: Central Government approval is the Schedule II route. It does not reach Schedule I items.

options.text: The remittance is prohibited, and no approval is available from any authority
options.explanation: Correct. Remittance out of lottery winnings is a Schedule I item. Schedule I drawals are prohibited outright, and neither the Reserve Bank nor the Central Government can approve them.

options.text: The remittance may be made with the prior approval of the Reserve Bank, on production of evidence of the winnings
options.explanation: RBI approval is the route for drawals above the Schedule III limits. Evidence of the source does not convert a prohibited item into an approvable one.

questions.topic: Ch 15 · Current Account Rules · Schedule II
questions.stem: A drawal of foreign exchange listed in Schedule II to the Current Account Transactions Rules 2000 — for example, remittance for a cultural tour — requires:
questions.sourceRef: Current Account Transactions Rules 2000, Schedule II (rules-level)

readLink.label: Read: Current account transactions — s. 5 and the Rules of 2000 →

options.text: No approval, the drawal being free up to the Liberalised Remittance Scheme ceiling
options.explanation: That is the Schedule III position. Schedule II items need an approval whatever the amount involved.

options.text: The prior approval of the Reserve Bank of India
options.explanation: The RBI is the approving authority for drawals exceeding the Schedule III limits, not for Schedule II items.

options.text: The prior approval of the Appellate Tribunal constituted under the Act
options.explanation: The Tribunal is an appellate body in adjudication proceedings. It has no role in permitting remittances.

options.text: The prior approval of the Central Government, of the Ministry or Department administering the subject
options.explanation: Correct. Schedule II items are drawals permitted only with the prior approval of the Central Government, through the Ministry or Department concerned with the subject matter — the Ministry dealing with culture in the case of a cultural tour.

questions.topic: Ch 15 · Schedule III · Nature of the LRS ceiling
questions.stem: Which statement about the Liberalised Remittance Scheme ceiling applicable to Schedule III drawals is correct?
questions.sourceRef: Current Account Transactions Rules 2000, Schedule III read with the RBI's LRS (rules and circular level)

readLink.label: Read: Current account transactions — s. 5 and the Rules of 2000 →

options.text: It is a ceiling of USD 2,50,000 per financial year for each resident individual, covering permissible current and capital account drawals taken together, and it does not carry forward
options.explanation: Correct. The ceiling is personal to each resident individual, runs by financial year, is consumed by current and capital account drawals alike, and unused headroom lapses at the end of the year.

options.text: It is a ceiling of USD 2,50,000 per financial year for each resident family, to be shared among its members
options.explanation: There is no family ceiling. Each resident individual, including a minor, has a separate ceiling; a minor's form is signed by a guardian.

options.text: It is a ceiling of USD 2,50,000 for each transaction, so any number of transactions may be undertaken in a year
options.explanation: This turns an annual aggregate into a per-transaction limit. The drawals in the year are aggregated against the single ceiling.

options.text: It applies only to current account transactions; capital account drawals such as the purchase of shares abroad are outside it
options.explanation: The scheme is deliberately combined. Buying shares or immovable property abroad draws on the same ceiling as travel, gifts and education remittances.

questions.stem: During the financial year 2026-27 Mr Ranjit Bose, a resident individual, has already remitted USD 90,000 towards his son's tuition fees in Melbourne and USD 35,000 as a gift to a nephew abroad. Taking the Liberalised Remittance Scheme ceiling at USD 2,50,000 per financial year, the amount he may still remit in that year without the prior approval of the Reserve Bank is:
questions.sourceRef: Current Account Transactions Rules 2000, Schedule III read with the LRS ceiling of USD 2,50,000 (amendment-sensitive)

readLink.label: Read: Current account transactions — s. 5 and the Rules of 2000 →

options.explanation: This ignores the drawals already made. The ceiling is an annual aggregate, so earlier remittances in the same financial year reduce the headroom.
Correct. Drawals so far are 90,000 + 35,000 = USD 1,25,000; headroom is 2,50,000 − 1,25,000 = USD 1,25,000. Anything beyond that in FY 2026-27 needs prior RBI approval.
This counts only the tuition remittance (2,50,000 − 90,000). The gift is equally a Schedule III drawal and must be counted.
This counts only the gift (2,50,000 − 35,000). Education remittances are within the scheme and consume the same ceiling.

questions.stem: In the financial year 2026-27 Mrs Sunanda Pillai, a resident individual, has remitted USD 1,20,000 for medical treatment abroad, USD 48,000 for private visits and USD 25,000 as a donation to a foreign charity. No amount has been remitted beyond the ceiling on the strength of any estimate. With the Liberalised Remittance Scheme ceiling at USD 2,50,000, her remaining headroom for the year is:
questions.sourceRef: Current Account Transactions Rules 2000, Schedule III read with the LRS ceiling of USD 2,50,000 (amendment-sensitive)

readLink.label: Read: Current account transactions — s. 5 and the Rules of 2000 →

options.explanation: This leaves the medical remittance out of the aggregate. Medical treatment may be remitted above the ceiling on a hospital's estimate, but the stem says no such estimate was used, so the USD 1,20,000 counts in full.
This omits the donation (2,50,000 − 1,20,000 − 48,000). A donation is a Schedule III drawal and consumes the ceiling.
Correct. Total drawals are 1,20,000 + 48,000 + 25,000 = USD 1,93,000, so headroom is 2,50,000 − 1,93,000 = USD 57,000.
This counts only the medical remittance (2,50,000 − 1,20,000) and ignores the private visits and the donation.

questions.topic: Ch 15 · Schedule III · Drawals above the ceiling
questions.stem: Which of the following purposes may NOT be remitted in excess of the Liberalised Remittance Scheme ceiling merely on the strength of supporting documentation, and instead requires the prior approval of the Reserve Bank for the excess?
questions.sourceRef: Current Account Transactions Rules 2000, Schedule III (rules-level)

readLink.label: Read: Current account transactions — s. 5 and the Rules of 2000 →

options.text: Studies abroad, where the institution's estimate is for a higher amount
options.explanation: Studies abroad is one of the documented exceptions: a higher amount may be remitted where the institution's estimate supports it.

options.text: Medical treatment abroad, where the hospital's estimate is for a higher amount
options.explanation: Medical treatment is likewise a documented exception; the estimate from the hospital or doctor abroad supports the higher remittance.

options.text: Emigration, where the country of emigration requires a higher amount
options.explanation: Emigration is treated in the same way, the requirement of the country of emigration supporting the higher figure.

options.text: A gift or donation to a person or institution abroad
options.explanation: Correct. A gift or donation has no documented exception. It is capped at the ceiling, and anything beyond it needs the prior approval of the Reserve Bank — which is why an over-ceiling gift is the standard exam trap.

questions.stem: Following the amendment of section 6 of FEMA 1999, the power to specify permissible classes of capital account transactions, the limits and the conditions is divided as follows:

readLink.label: Read: Capital account transactions — section 6 →

options.text: The Reserve Bank, in consultation with the Central Government, for transactions involving debt instruments; and the Central Government, in consultation with the Reserve Bank, for transactions not involving debt instruments
options.explanation: Correct. Section 6(2) gives debt instruments to the Reserve Bank and s. 6(2A) gives non-debt instruments to the Central Government, each acting in consultation with the other. What is a debt instrument is determined by the Central Government in consultation with the RBI under s. 6(7).

options.text: The Central Government for debt instruments and the Reserve Bank for non-debt instruments
options.explanation: The split is real but stated the wrong way round. Debt sits with the Reserve Bank.

options.text: The Reserve Bank alone, for all capital account transactions, as before the amendment
options.explanation: That was the pre-2015 position. The amendment created the debt / non-debt division and moved non-debt instruments to the Central Government.

options.text: The Central Government alone, for all capital account transactions, the Reserve Bank retaining only current account powers
options.explanation: This inverts the whole scheme. Current account restrictions are the Central Government's under s. 5; the RBI retains the debt limb of the capital account under s. 6(2).

questions.stem: Mr Faisal Qureshi worked in Dubai from 2014 to 2025 as a person resident outside India and, during that period, bought an apartment there and acquired shares in a UAE company. He returns permanently to India and becomes a person resident in India. Under FEMA:

readLink.label: Read: Capital account transactions — section 6 →

options.text: He must dispose of both the apartment and the shares and repatriate the proceeds, section 4 prohibiting a resident from holding immovable property or securities outside India
options.explanation: Section 4 alone would say so, but s. 6(4) is the express exception for assets acquired while the person was resident outside India.

options.text: He may continue to hold, own, transfer or invest in both, because they were acquired when he was a person resident outside India
options.explanation: Correct. Section 6(4) permits a person resident in India to hold, own, transfer or invest in foreign currency, foreign security or immovable property situated outside India where these were acquired, held or owned by him when he was resident outside India, or inherited from a person who was resident outside India.

options.text: He may retain the shares but must dispose of the immovable property, section 6(4) covering only securities
options.explanation: Section 6(4) names foreign currency, foreign security and immovable property situated outside India in the same breath. There is no distinction between them.

options.text: He may retain both only with the prior approval of the Central Government, obtained within 180 days of his return
options.explanation: No approval and no 180-day window exist for this. The protection in s. 6(4) is automatic and needs no application.

questions.stem: Under section 7(1)(a) of FEMA 1999, an exporter of goods must furnish a declaration containing true and correct material particulars including:

readLink.label: Read: Export, realisation and exemptions — ss. 7, 8 and 9 →

options.text: The cost of production of the goods, so that the authority may satisfy itself as to the margin earned
options.explanation: Cost and margin are irrelevant to s. 7. The declaration is concerned with the value expected to be realised from abroad.

options.text: The identity of the overseas buyer and his banker, but not any value
options.explanation: Buyer particulars may be called for as 'such other information' under s. 7(1)(b), but the section expressly requires the export value in the declaration itself.

options.text: The amount representing the full export value of the goods or, where the full export value is not ascertainable at the time of export, the value which the exporter, having regard to prevailing market conditions, expects to receive on a sale in a market outside India
options.explanation: Correct. Section 7(1)(a) requires the full export value and provides the expected-value alternative where the full value cannot be ascertained at the time of export.

options.text: An undertaking that the proceeds will be realised within six months, that period being fixed by the section
options.explanation: The realisation period is fixed by the Reserve Bank's regulations under s. 8, not by s. 7, and no period is stated in the Act at all.

questions.stem: Section 8 of FEMA 1999 obliges a person resident in India to whom foreign exchange is due or has accrued to:

readLink.label: Read: Export, realisation and exemptions — ss. 7, 8 and 9 →

options.text: Guarantee realisation of the amount, failure to recover being itself a contravention
options.explanation: The section imposes a standard of conduct, not a guarantee of result. An exporter who has genuinely pursued a defaulting buyer has complied.

options.text: Realise the amount within six months, that period being fixed by the section itself
options.explanation: The period is 'such period as the Reserve Bank may specify', which sits in the regulations and has been changed. The Act names no period.

options.text: Realise and repatriate the amount only if it exceeds the limit specified in section 9
options.explanation: Section 9 lists exempt categories, each subject to an RBI limit. It is not a general threshold below which s. 8 does not apply.

options.text: Take all reasonable steps to realise and repatriate it to India within such period and in such manner as the Reserve Bank may specify, save as otherwise provided or with the RBI's permission
options.explanation: Correct. The duty is to take all reasonable steps; the period and manner are specified by the RBI; and 'repatriate' carries its s. 2(y) meaning of selling the exchange to an authorised person or holding it in a permitted account.

questions.stem: The Reserve Bank proposes to revoke the authorisation of an authorised person. Which statement correctly describes the requirement of a hearing?

readLink.label: Read: Authorised persons — sections 10 to 12 →

options.text: Where revocation is proposed on the ground of failure to comply with the conditions or of contravention of the Act, the authorised person must first be given a reasonable opportunity of making a representation; where it is proposed in the public interest, no such opportunity is required
options.explanation: Correct. The proviso to s. 10(3) attaches the representation requirement only to the non-compliance and contravention ground. Revocation in the public interest is not conditioned on a representation.

options.text: A reasonable opportunity of making a representation is required in every case, whatever the ground
options.explanation: This ignores the wording of the proviso, which is confined to the second ground.

options.text: No opportunity is required on any ground, revocation being an administrative act of the Reserve Bank
options.explanation: The proviso expressly requires a representation where the ground is non-compliance or contravention.

options.text: An opportunity is required only where revocation is proposed in the public interest, since that ground involves no fault of the authorised person
options.explanation: This reverses the proviso. The fault-based ground carries the procedural protection; the public-interest ground does not.

questions.topic: Ch 15 · s. 10(6) · Deemed contravention by the drawer
questions.stem: Mr Suraj Dixit, a resident individual, buys USD 20,000 from an authorised dealer declaring the purpose as a private visit abroad. He then cancels the trip, does not use the foreign exchange for the declared purpose and does not surrender it within the specified period. Under FEMA:

readLink.label: Read: Authorised persons — sections 10 to 12 →

options.text: There is no contravention, because the original drawal was lawful and he has done nothing further
options.explanation: Section 10(6) is aimed exactly at this situation. The lawfulness of the drawal depended on the declared purpose, and abandoning it without surrendering the exchange is a deemed contravention.

options.text: He is deemed to have committed a contravention of the Act, because he has neither used the foreign exchange for the declared purpose nor surrendered it to an authorised person within the specified period
options.explanation: Correct. Section 10(6) deems a contravention where a person who acquired foreign exchange for a declared purpose does not use it for that purpose, does not surrender it within the specified period, or uses it for a purpose for which acquisition is not permissible.

options.text: Only the authorised dealer is liable, for having failed to monitor the use of the foreign exchange sold
options.explanation: The dealer's duties under s. 10(5) are to take a declaration, refuse in writing and report on reasonable belief. Section 10(6) fastens on the customer.

options.text: The contravention arises only if he uses the foreign exchange for an impermissible purpose; mere retention is not caught
options.explanation: Retention is expressly caught by the second limb of s. 10(6) — failure to surrender within the specified period is itself a deemed contravention.

questions.topic: Ch 15 · s. 11(3) · Penalty on an authorised person
questions.stem: An authorised person fails to file a return that the Reserve Bank has directed him to file. After giving him a reasonable opportunity of being heard, the Reserve Bank may impose on him a penalty which may extend to:

readLink.label: Read: Authorised persons — sections 10 to 12 →

options.text: Thrice the sum involved in the contravention, or ₹2,00,000 where the sum is not quantifiable
options.explanation: That is the general adjudicated penalty under s. 13, imposed by an Adjudicating Authority on any person. Section 11(3) is a distinct and much smaller RBI penalty on an authorised person.

options.text: ₹2,00,000, with a further ₹5,000 for every day of a continuing contravention
options.explanation: Again the s. 13 figures. The examiner's trap is to attach them to an authorised person's breach of a direction or failure to file a return.

options.text: ₹10,000, and in the case of a continuing contravention a further penalty which may extend to ₹2,000 for every day during which the contravention continues
options.explanation: Correct. Section 11(3) provides a penalty up to ₹10,000, with an additional penalty up to ₹2,000 for every day of continuance, imposed by the Reserve Bank after a reasonable opportunity of being heard.

options.text: ₹10,000 only, no continuing penalty being provided for a failure to file a return
options.explanation: The continuing-day penalty of up to ₹2,000 is expressly provided by s. 11(3) and applies to a continuing contravention.

questions.topic: Ch 15 · s. 13(1) · Thrice the sum involved
questions.stem: On adjudication, Mr Tanmay Ghosh is found to have contravened section 3 of FEMA 1999 in respect of a transaction of ₹42,00,000. The contravention is complete on a single day and the amount involved is quantifiable. The maximum penalty that may be imposed under section 13(1) is:
questions.sourceRef: FEMA 1999, s. 13(1) — penalty up to thrice the sum involved

readLink.label: Read: Contravention and penalty — section 13 →

options.explanation: That is the sum involved itself. Section 13(1) allows a penalty up to three times that amount where the sum is quantifiable.
That is twice the sum involved. The statutory multiple is three, not two.
₹2,00,000 is the maximum only where the amount involved is not quantifiable. Here it is quantifiable, so the thrice-the-sum limb applies.
Correct. 3 × ₹42,00,000 = ₹1,26,00,000. Note that this is a maximum — the Adjudicating Authority may impose less, the section reading 'which may extend to'.

questions.stem: An Adjudicating Authority finds a contravention of FEMA in which the amount involved is not quantifiable. The contravention is a continuing one and has continued for 40 days after the first day. The maximum penalty that may be imposed under section 13(1) is:
questions.sourceRef: FEMA 1999, s. 13(1) — ₹2,00,000 where not quantifiable, plus ₹5,000 per day after the first day

readLink.label: Read: Contravention and penalty — section 13 →

options.explanation: Correct. The base maximum where the amount is not quantifiable is ₹2,00,000; the continuing penalty is 40 × ₹5,000 = ₹2,00,000; total ₹4,00,000.
This applies only the base maximum and ignores the continuing-day penalty that s. 13(1) adds for every day after the first day.
This counts 41 days of continuance. The section counts days after the first day, so 40 days at ₹5,000 gives ₹2,00,000.
This adds the continuing penalty once instead of for each of the 40 days.

questions.stem: A contravention of FEMA involves a quantifiable sum of ₹18,50,000 and is a continuing contravention which has continued for 25 days after the first day. The maximum aggregate penalty under section 13(1) is:
questions.sourceRef: FEMA 1999, s. 13(1) — thrice the sum involved plus ₹5,000 per day after the first day

readLink.label: Read: Contravention and penalty — section 13 →

options.explanation: This is 3 × ₹18,50,000 and stops there. The continuing-day penalty of ₹5,000 per day after the first day must be added.
This adds the continuing penalty to the sum involved without trebling it. The base for a quantifiable contravention is three times the sum.
This counts 26 continuing days. Days are counted after the first day, giving 25 at ₹5,000.

questions.topic: Ch 15 · s. 14 · Ninety days from the demand notice
questions.stem: A penalty imposed on Mr Iqbal Ansari under section 13 is the subject of a notice for payment served on him on 10 June 2026. He becomes liable to civil imprisonment under section 14 only if he fails to make full payment by:
questions.sourceRef: FEMA 1999, s. 14(1) — 90 days from the date of service of the notice for payment

readLink.label: Read: Enforcement, compounding and the appellate ladder →

options.text: 25 July 2026
options.explanation: That is 45 days from service. Forty-five days is the appeal window under ss. 17 and 19, not the payment period under s. 14.

options.text: 10 September 2026
options.explanation: That is three calendar months from 10 June. Section 14 speaks of 90 days, which is counted day by day and falls two days earlier.

options.text: 8 September 2026
options.explanation: Correct. Ninety days counted from 10 June 2026 ends on 8 September 2026. Only failure to pay in full by that date attracts liability to civil imprisonment, and even then only after a show-cause notice from the Adjudicating Authority.

options.text: 7 December 2026
options.explanation: That is 180 days from service — the compounding period under s. 15, not the payment period under s. 14.

questions.stem: An application for compounding of a contravention is received by the compounding authority on 12 May 2026. Under section 15(1) of FEMA 1999 the contravention is to be compounded on or before:
questions.sourceRef: FEMA 1999, s. 15(1) — 180 days from the date of receipt of the application

readLink.label: Read: Enforcement, compounding and the appellate ladder →

options.text: 12 November 2026
options.explanation: That is six calendar months. Section 15(1) fixes 180 days, which is counted day by day and expires four days earlier.

options.text: 10 August 2026
options.explanation: That is 90 days from receipt — the s. 14 payment period, not the compounding period.

options.text: 26 June 2026
options.explanation: That is 45 days, the appeal window under ss. 17 and 19.

options.text: 8 November 2026
options.explanation: Correct. One hundred and eighty days from 12 May 2026 ends on 8 November 2026. The clock runs from the date of receipt of the application, not from the contravention or from any notice.

questions.topic: Ch 15 · s. 35 · Appeal to the High Court
questions.stem: An order of the Appellate Tribunal is communicated to Sanchita Exports LLP on 3 December 2026. Without seeking any extension, the last date on which it may file an appeal to the High Court on a question of law under section 35 of FEMA 1999 is:
questions.sourceRef: FEMA 1999, s. 35 — 60 days from the date of communication of the order

readLink.label: Read: Enforcement, compounding and the appellate ladder →

options.text: 1 February 2027
options.explanation: Correct. Sixty days from 3 December 2026 ends on 1 February 2027. On sufficient cause the High Court may allow a further period not exceeding sixty days, but that is an extension and not the ordinary window.

options.text: 17 January 2027
options.explanation: That is 45 days — the window for an appeal to the Special Director (Appeals) under s. 17 or to the Appellate Tribunal under s. 19, not to the High Court.

options.text: 3 February 2027
options.explanation: That is two calendar months. Section 35 speaks of sixty days, counted day by day.

options.text: 3 March 2027
options.explanation: That is 90 days. No 90-day appeal period exists under FEMA; the outer limit with the maximum extension would in any event be 60 + 60 days.

questions.stem: A contravention of FEMA is committed by a company. Under section 42, which of the following statements is correct?

readLink.label: Read: Directorate of Enforcement, presumptions and offences by companies →

options.text: Every director of the company is automatically liable, no defence being available to any of them
options.explanation: Neither limb works that way. Sub-section (1) reaches the person in charge of and responsible for the conduct of the business and allows a defence; sub-section (2) requires consent, connivance or neglect to be established.

options.text: The company, and every person who at the time of the contravention was in charge of and was responsible to the company for the conduct of its business, are liable — but such a person escapes on proving that the contravention took place without his knowledge or that he exercised all due diligence to prevent it
options.explanation: Correct. That is s. 42(1) with its proviso. Section 42(2) then adds, separately, any director, manager, secretary or other officer with whose consent or connivance the contravention was committed or to whose neglect it is attributable.

options.text: Section 42 applies only to companies incorporated under the Companies Act 2013, partnership firms being outside it
options.explanation: The Explanation defines 'company' to mean any body corporate and to include a firm or other association of individuals, and defines 'director' in relation to a firm as a partner in the firm.

options.text: An officer is liable under section 42(2) only if he was also in charge of and responsible for the conduct of the business
options.explanation: That condition belongs to sub-section (1). Sub-section (2) operates independently, on proof of consent, connivance or neglect, and can catch an officer who was never in charge of the business.

questions.topic: Ch 15 · s. 2(v) · Person resident in India
questions.stem: Explain the meaning of 'person resident in India' under section 2(v) of the Foreign Exchange Management Act 1999. Mr Arvind Menon, an Indian citizen, left India on 2 May 2025 to take up employment in Doha and returned to India permanently on 12 March 2026. Determine his residential status under FEMA for the financial years 2025-26 and 2026-27, giving reasons. (5 marks)

skeleton.point: Basic rule in s. 2(v)(i): a person residing in India for more than one hundred and eighty-two days during the course of the PRECEDING financial year is a person resident in India; 'more than 182' means 183 days or more, and the financial year runs from 1 April to 31 March

The two exclusions that override the day count: (A) a person who has gone out of India or stays outside India for or on taking up employment outside India, for carrying on business or vocation outside India, or for any other purpose in circumstances indicating an intention to stay outside India for an uncertain period, is NOT a person resident in India; and (B) a person who has come to or stays in India OTHERWISE THAN for employment, business or vocation in India, or for a purpose indicating an intention to stay for an uncertain period, is also NOT a person resident in India

The remaining limbs of s. 2(v): any person or body corporate registered or incorporated in India; an office, branch or agency in India owned or controlled by a person resident outside India; and an office, branch or agency outside India owned or controlled by a person resident in India — each is a person resident in India; a person resident outside India is defined residually by s. 2(w)

Application: for FY 2025-26 Mr Menon went out of India on 2 May 2025 for employment outside India, so exclusion (A) applies and he is a person resident OUTSIDE India from his departure, whatever his day count; for FY 2026-27 he returned on 12 March 2026 with the intention of staying permanently — a stay in India for an uncertain period, so exclusion (B) does not save him, and his status follows the ordinary rule and his purpose of return, making him a person resident IN India; the conclusion must be reasoned from the PURPOSE first and the day count second
skeleton.citation: FEMA 1999, s. 2(v) — application to the facts

questions.topic: Ch 15 · ss. 2(e), 2(j), 5 and 6 · Capital and current account transactions
questions.stem: Distinguish between a 'capital account transaction' and a 'current account transaction' under the Foreign Exchange Management Act 1999, and explain how the Act treats each. Classify, with reasons, (i) payment of interest on an external commercial borrowing, (ii) repayment of the principal of that borrowing, and (iii) the purchase of a flat in Dubai by a person resident in India. (6 marks)

skeleton.point: Capital account transaction, s. 2(e): a transaction which alters the assets or liabilities, including contingent liabilities, outside India of persons resident in India, or the assets or liabilities in India of persons resident outside India, and includes the transactions referred to in section 6(3)

Current account transaction, s. 2(j): a transaction OTHER THAN a capital account transaction — a residual definition — and, without prejudice to that generality, includes payments due in connection with foreign trade, other current business, services and short-term banking and credit facilities in the ordinary course of business; payments due as interest on loans and as net income from investments; remittances for living expenses of parents, spouse and children residing abroad; and expenses in connection with foreign travel, education and medical care of parents, spouse and children

Treatment: under s. 5 any person may sell or draw foreign exchange to or from an authorised person for a CURRENT account transaction, subject only to reasonable restrictions imposed by the Central Government by rules, in the public interest and in consultation with the Reserve Bank — the default is freedom; under s. 6 a CAPITAL account transaction is permitted only within the classes, limits and conditions specified by the Reserve Bank (debt instruments, s. 6(2)) or prescribed by the Central Government (non-debt instruments, s. 6(2A)) — the default is restriction
(i) Interest on an external commercial borrowing: no cross-border asset or liability is altered, and interest on loans is expressly included in s. 2(j)(ii) — a CURRENT account transaction

(ii) Repayment of the principal: it extinguishes a liability outside India of a person resident in India and is therefore a CAPITAL account transaction — the same loan generates transactions of both kinds

(iii) Purchase of a flat in Dubai by a resident: it creates an asset outside India of a person resident in India and is a CAPITAL account transaction; it must fall within a permissible class and, for a resident individual, draws on the Liberalised Remittance Scheme ceiling
skeleton.citation: FEMA 1999, ss. 2(e) and 6, read with Schedule III and the LRS (rules-level)

questions.topic: Ch 15 · s. 5 · The Current Account Transactions Rules 2000
questions.stem: Section 5 of the Foreign Exchange Management Act 1999 declares current account transactions to be free, subject to reasonable restrictions. Explain the scheme of the Foreign Exchange Management (Current Account Transactions) Rules 2000, identifying the approving authority for each Schedule, and state the position of a resident individual who wishes to remit an amount exceeding the Liberalised Remittance Scheme ceiling as a gift. (5 marks)

skeleton.point: Section 5 and its proviso: any person may sell or draw foreign exchange to or from an authorised person if the sale or drawal is a current account transaction; the Central Government may, in the public interest and in consultation with the Reserve Bank, impose reasonable restrictions by rules — hence the Current Account Transactions Rules 2000, which are Government rules and not RBI regulations

Schedule I — drawal of foreign exchange is PROHIBITED and no approval is available from any authority; illustrations include remittance out of lottery winnings, income from racing, riding or any hobby, remittance for the purchase of lottery tickets, sweepstakes or banned or proscribed magazines, payment of commission on exports towards equity investment in Indian joint ventures or wholly-owned subsidiaries abroad, payment related to a 'call-back services' telephone arrangement, and remittance of interest income on funds held in a Non-Resident Special Rupee Account
skeleton.citation: Current Account Transactions Rules 2000, Schedule I (rules-level, amendment-sensitive)

skeleton.point: Schedule II — drawal requires the PRIOR APPROVAL OF THE CENTRAL GOVERNMENT, of the Ministry or Department administering the subject; illustrations include cultural tours, advertisement in foreign print media above the prescribed threshold for purposes other than promotion of tourism, foreign investments and international bidding, remittance of freight on a vessel chartered by a public sector undertaking, hiring of transponders, remittance of prize money or sponsorship of a sports activity abroad above the threshold, and payment for securing health insurance from a company abroad
skeleton.citation: Current Account Transactions Rules 2000, Schedule II (rules-level, amendment-sensitive)

skeleton.point: Schedule III — drawal is FREE UP TO A LIMIT and requires the PRIOR APPROVAL OF THE RESERVE BANK beyond it; the limit is the Liberalised Remittance Scheme ceiling of USD 2,50,000 per financial year per resident individual, covering current and capital account drawals together and not carried forward; the named purposes include private visits other than to Nepal and Bhutan, gift or donation, going abroad for employment, emigration, maintenance of close relatives abroad, business travel or conference or specialised training, medical treatment abroad and studies abroad
skeleton.citation: Current Account Transactions Rules 2000, Schedule III read with the LRS ceiling (amendment-sensitive)

skeleton.point: Application to a gift above the ceiling: studies, medical treatment, emigration and maintenance of close relatives may exceed the ceiling on the strength of an estimate or requirement, but a GIFT OR DONATION has no such documented exception — the excess may be remitted only with the prior approval of the Reserve Bank, and an authorised person is bound to refuse the drawal without it
skeleton.citation: Current Account Transactions Rules 2000, Schedule III (rules-level)

questions.stem: State the duties of an authorised person under the Foreign Exchange Management Act 1999 and the consequences of a breach, and explain the position of a customer who acquires foreign exchange from an authorised person for a declared purpose and then fails to use it for that purpose. (4 marks)

skeleton.point: Authorisation and its revocation: the Reserve Bank may, on application, authorise a person as an authorised dealer, money changer, off-shore banking unit or otherwise, by an authorisation in writing subject to conditions; it may revoke the authorisation at any time in the public interest, or for failure to comply with the conditions or for contravention of the Act, rules, regulations, notifications, directions or orders — the second ground requiring a reasonable opportunity of making a representation

Duties in dealing: to comply with the Reserve Bank's general or special directions or orders, and not to engage, without the RBI's previous permission, in any transaction involving foreign exchange or a foreign security which is not in conformity with the terms of the authorisation

Duty of enquiry: before undertaking a transaction, to require the customer to make such declaration and give such information as will reasonably satisfy the authorised person that the transaction will not involve, and is not designed for the purpose of, any contravention or evasion of the Act, rules or regulations; on refusal or unsatisfactory compliance, to refuse in writing to undertake the transaction and, where he has reason to believe that a contravention or evasion is contemplated, to report the matter to the Reserve Bank

Consequences and the customer's position: an authorised person who contravenes a direction of the Reserve Bank or fails to file a prescribed return is liable, after a reasonable opportunity of being heard, to a penalty up to ₹10,000 with a further penalty up to ₹2,000 for every day of continuance (s. 11(3)), and is subject to inspection by the Reserve Bank (s. 12); a person other than an authorised person who acquires foreign exchange for a declared purpose and does not use it for that purpose, does not surrender it to an authorised person within the specified period, or uses it for a purpose for which acquisition is not permissible, is DEEMED to have committed a contravention (s. 10(6))

questions.topic: Ch 15 · ss. 13 to 15 · Penalty, confiscation, enforcement and compounding
questions.stem: Explain the penalty provisions of section 13 of the Foreign Exchange Management Act 1999, the power of confiscation, the consequence of failing to pay a penalty, and the compounding of contraventions. Ganga Traders is adjudged to have contravened section 3 in respect of a transaction of ₹30,00,000, the contravention having continued for 60 days after the first day. Compute the maximum penalty. (6 marks)

skeleton.point: Section 13(1): a person who contravenes any provision of the Act, or any rule, regulation, notification, direction or order issued under it, or any condition subject to which an authorisation is issued by the Reserve Bank, shall UPON ADJUDICATION be liable to a penalty which may extend to thrice the sum involved where that amount is quantifiable, or to ₹2,00,000 where it is not quantifiable, and, where the contravention is a continuing one, to a further penalty which may extend to ₹5,000 for every day AFTER THE FIRST DAY during which the contravention continues; every figure is a maximum

Section 13(2): in addition to any penalty, the Adjudicating Authority may direct that the currency, security or any other money or property in respect of which the contravention has taken place be confiscated to the Central Government, and may further direct that the person's foreign exchange holdings be brought back into India or retained outside India in accordance with its directions; the Explanation extends 'property' to bank deposits, Indian currency or other property into which the property has been converted

Section 14: where a person fails to make full payment of the penalty within 90 days from the date on which the notice for payment is served on him, he is liable to civil imprisonment; no order for arrest and detention may be made unless the Adjudicating Authority has issued and served a notice calling on him to appear and show cause why he should not be committed to civil prison and has heard him; detention may extend to three years where the demand exceeds ₹1 crore and to six months in any other case, and detention does not discharge the liability to pay

Section 15: any contravention under s. 13 may, on an application by the person committing it, be compounded WITHIN 180 DAYS FROM THE DATE OF RECEIPT OF THE APPLICATION by the Director of Enforcement or such other officers of the Directorate of Enforcement and of the Reserve Bank as may be authorised; where a contravention has been compounded, no proceeding or further proceeding shall be initiated or continued against that person under s. 13 in respect of the contravention so compounded; under the compounding rules, contraventions of s. 3(a) are compounded by the Directorate of Enforcement and other contraventions by the Reserve Bank
skeleton.citation: FEMA 1999, s. 15 read with the Foreign Exchange (Compounding Proceedings) Rules 2000 (rules-level)

skeleton.point: Computation for Ganga Traders: the sum involved is quantifiable at ₹30,00,000, so the base maximum is 3 × ₹30,00,000 = ₹90,00,000; the continuing penalty is 60 days × ₹5,000 = ₹3,00,000; the maximum aggregate penalty is therefore ₹93,00,000, subject in addition to confiscation under s. 13(2); the answer must state that these are maxima and that the Adjudicating Authority may impose less
skeleton.citation: FEMA 1999, s. 13(1) — application to the facts

questions.topic: Ch 15 · ss. 16 to 19 and 35 · Adjudication and appeals
questions.stem: Describe the adjudication machinery under the Foreign Exchange Management Act 1999 and the appellate remedies available against an order of an Adjudicating Authority, stating the time limits in each case. (4 marks)

skeleton.point: Adjudication, s. 16: the Central Government appoints officers of the Directorate of Enforcement as Adjudicating Authorities to hold an enquiry into contraventions; the enquiry may be held only upon a complaint in writing made by an officer authorised by a general or special order of the Central Government; the person is given a reasonable opportunity of being heard and may appear in person or take the assistance of a legal practitioner or a CHARTERED ACCOUNTANT of his choice; the Adjudicating Authority shall endeavour to dispose of the complaint within one year of its receipt, recording reasons in writing where it does not

First appeal, s. 17: an appeal against an order of an Adjudicating Authority who is an Assistant Director or a Deputy Director of Enforcement lies to the SPECIAL DIRECTOR (APPEALS) within 45 DAYS from the date on which a copy of the order is received by the aggrieved person; the Special Director (Appeals) may entertain an appeal after that period if satisfied that there was sufficient cause for the delay

Appeal to the Appellate Tribunal, s. 19: an appeal against an order of an Adjudicating Authority above that rank, or against an order of the Special Director (Appeals), lies to the APPELLATE TRIBUNAL within 45 DAYS from the date on which a copy of the order is received, with power to condone delay on sufficient cause; the appeal is entertained only on deposit of the penalty, though the Tribunal may dispense with the deposit, subject to conditions, where it is of the opinion that the deposit would cause undue hardship; the Tribunal shall endeavour to dispose of the appeal within 180 days of receipt
skeleton.citation: FEMA 1999, s. 19 and the proviso to s. 19(1)

skeleton.point: Appeal to the High Court, s. 35: any person aggrieved by a decision or order of the Appellate Tribunal may appeal to the HIGH COURT within 60 DAYS from the date of communication of the decision or order, but ONLY ON A QUESTION OF LAW arising out of it; the High Court may, on being satisfied that the appellant was prevented by sufficient cause, allow the appeal to be filed within a further period not exceeding 60 days

questions.topic: Ch 15 · Case: a family's remittances in one financial year
questions.case: Nandita Varma and her husband Rohit are both persons resident in India, living in Pune. During the financial year 2026-27 the following drawals of foreign exchange are proposed through their authorised dealer. (1) Nandita remits USD 62,000 to her daughter's university in Boston towards tuition and hostel charges; the university's estimate for the year is exactly USD 62,000. (2) Rohit draws USD 18,000 for a business trip to Japan to negotiate a supply contract for the firm in which he is a partner. (3) Nandita remits USD 2,05,000 to her sister in London as a gift towards the purchase of a house; no estimate or requirement of any institution supports the amount. (4) Nandita also asks the bank to remit USD 15,000, being her winnings from an overseas lottery, to the same sister. Assume the Liberalised Remittance Scheme ceiling is USD 2,50,000 per financial year per resident individual.

readLink.label: Read: Current account transactions — s. 5 and the Rules of 2000 →

questions.stem: The gift of USD 2,05,000 by Nandita to her sister is, in its nature:

options.text: A capital account transaction, because it is a large one-time transfer of value out of India
options.explanation: Size is not the test. Section 2(e) asks whether cross-border assets or liabilities are altered, and a gift alters neither for the giver or the receiver in the relevant sense.

options.text: A capital account transaction, because a gift is not one of the four groups listed in section 2(j)
options.explanation: The four groups in s. 2(j) are illustrations. The definition is residual, so absence from the list decides nothing.

options.text: A current account transaction, because it is not a capital account transaction within section 2(e)
options.explanation: Correct. Section 2(j) defines a current account transaction as any transaction other than a capital account transaction. The gift creates no asset or liability across the border, so it falls into the residual class — and is then restricted only by the Schedule III limit.

options.text: Neither, since gifts between relatives are outside the scope of FEMA altogether
options.explanation: FEMA recognises no such exemption for gifts, and no third class of transaction exists.

questions.stem: Ignoring item (4), by how much do Nandita's own proposed drawals for the financial year 2026-27 exceed the Liberalised Remittance Scheme ceiling, so as to require the prior approval of the Reserve Bank?
questions.sourceRef: Current Account Transactions Rules 2000, Schedule III read with the LRS ceiling of USD 2,50,000 (amendment-sensitive)

options.text: Nil — her drawals are within the ceiling
options.explanation: Her two drawals aggregate USD 2,67,000, which is above the ceiling of USD 2,50,000.

Correct. Nandita's drawals are 62,000 + 2,05,000 = USD 2,67,000; the excess over the USD 2,50,000 ceiling is USD 17,000. Because the excess is attributable to a gift, which has no documented exception, that USD 17,000 needs the prior approval of the Reserve Bank.
This adds Rohit's USD 18,000 to Nandita's drawals. The ceiling is per resident individual, so his drawal runs against his own separate ceiling.

USD 1,88,000 is the headroom available to Nandita after the education remittance (2,50,000 − 62,000). Headroom is not the same as excess; the excess is the amount by which the proposed gift overshoots that headroom.

questions.stem: As to item (4), the proposed remittance of USD 15,000 of overseas lottery winnings:
questions.sourceRef: Current Account Transactions Rules 2000, Schedule I (rules-level)

options.text: May be made freely, being well within the Liberalised Remittance Scheme ceiling
options.explanation: The ceiling is irrelevant to a Schedule I item, which is prohibited whatever the amount.

options.text: May be made with the prior approval of the Reserve Bank, since it exceeds no limit
options.explanation: RBI approval is available for Schedule III drawals above the limit. It is not available for a prohibited item.

options.text: May be made with the prior approval of the Central Government department concerned
options.explanation: Central Government approval is the Schedule II route and does not reach Schedule I items.

options.text: Is prohibited, remittance out of lottery winnings being a Schedule I item for which no approval is available from any authority
options.explanation: Correct. Schedule I to the Current Account Transactions Rules 2000 prohibits the drawal outright. The bank must decline, and neither the Reserve Bank nor the Central Government can permit it.

questions.stem: As to item (2), Rohit's drawal of USD 18,000 for business travel:
questions.sourceRef: Current Account Transactions Rules 2000, Schedule III read with the LRS (rules-level)

options.text: Is free, being a Schedule III drawal within Rohit's own Liberalised Remittance Scheme ceiling, which is separate from Nandita's
options.explanation: Correct. The ceiling is per resident individual. Rohit has his own USD 2,50,000 for the financial year, and his business-travel drawal neither consumes Nandita's headroom nor is consumed by her drawals.

options.text: Must be aggregated with Nandita's drawals against a single family ceiling of USD 2,50,000
options.explanation: There is no family ceiling under the scheme. Each resident individual, including a minor, has a separate limit.

options.text: Requires the prior approval of the Central Government, business travel being a Schedule II item
options.explanation: Business travel, conference and specialised training are Schedule III items, free up to the limit. Schedule II items are a different list.

options.text: Is a capital account transaction, because it is undertaken for the purposes of a partnership firm
options.explanation: Travel expenses in the ordinary course of business alter no cross-border asset or liability, and are in any event within the illustrations in s. 2(j).

questions.topic: Ch 15 · Case: a payment outside the authorised channel
questions.case: Sunrise Metalworks Private Limited owes a supplier in Dubai for a consignment of components. Rather than remit through its bank, its finance director arranges for ₹63,00,000 in cash to be handed to an intermediary in Surat, whose associate abroad credits the equivalent in US dollars to the supplier's account in Dubai. No money crosses the border and no authorised person is involved in either leg. On information received, the Directorate of Enforcement investigates and an Adjudicating Authority holds the company to have contravened the Act in respect of the whole ₹63,00,000. The amount involved is quantifiable and the contravention is not a continuing one.

readLink.label: Read: Dealing in and holding foreign exchange — ss. 3 and 4 →

questions.stem: Which statement best identifies why the arrangement contravenes the Act?
questions.sourceRef: FEMA 1999, s. 3(a), (b) and (c) with the Explanation

options.text: Because payment for imported components is a capital account transaction requiring the prior approval of the Reserve Bank
options.explanation: Payment for goods already supplied discharges a trade payable and is a current account transaction under s. 2(j)(i). The classification is not the problem.

options.text: Because a private company may not make any payment to a person resident outside India without the approval of the Central Government
options.explanation: No such general bar exists. A company may pay an overseas supplier freely, provided it does so through an authorised person.

options.text: Because the amount involved exceeded the Liberalised Remittance Scheme ceiling applicable to the company
options.explanation: The Liberalised Remittance Scheme applies to resident individuals, not to companies, and the ceiling is not what this arrangement offends.

options.text: Because the payment bypassed an authorised person: section 3(a) and 3(b) are engaged, and the Explanation to section 3(c) deems a receipt without a corresponding inward remittance to be otherwise than through an authorised person
