options.explanation: Correct. The purpose of the payment was entirely permissible; the contravention lies in the channel. Each leg of the arrangement falls within s. 3, and the Explanation to clause (c) is what catches the payout abroad made without a matching inward remittance.

questions.stem: The maximum penalty that the Adjudicating Authority may impose on the company under section 13(1) in respect of this contravention is:
questions.sourceRef: FEMA 1999, s. 13(1) — penalty up to thrice the sum involved

options.explanation: That is the sum involved. The statutory maximum where the amount is quantifiable is three times that sum.
That is twice the sum involved. The multiple in s. 13(1) is three.
Correct. 3 × ₹63,00,000 = ₹1,89,00,000. As the contravention is not a continuing one, no daily penalty is added; and the figure is a ceiling, the Authority being free to impose less.
₹2,00,000 applies only where the amount involved is not quantifiable. Here it is quantifiable at ₹63,00,000.

questions.stem: The company applies for compounding of the contravention. The authority competent to compound it, and the period within which it is to be compounded, are:
questions.sourceRef: FEMA 1999, s. 15 read with the Foreign Exchange (Compounding Proceedings) Rules 2000 (rules-level)

options.text: The Directorate of Enforcement, within 180 days from the date of receipt of the application
options.explanation: Correct. Contraventions of s. 3(a) are compounded by the Directorate of Enforcement under the compounding rules, other contraventions being compounded by the Reserve Bank; and s. 15(1) requires the contravention to be compounded within 180 days of receipt of the application.

options.text: The Reserve Bank of India, within 180 days from the date of the contravention
options.explanation: Two errors: contraventions of s. 3(a) go to the Directorate of Enforcement, and the 180 days run from the receipt of the application, not from the contravention.

options.text: The Adjudicating Authority, within 90 days from the date of the adjudication order
options.explanation: Compounding is not a function of the Adjudicating Authority, and 90 days is the s. 14 payment period.

options.text: The Appellate Tribunal, within 45 days from the date of the order
options.explanation: The Tribunal hears appeals; it does not compound. Forty-five days is the appeal window under ss. 17 and 19.

questions.topic: Ch 15 · Case: adjudication, evidence and appeal
questions.case: Kapoor & Associates is a firm of exporters with four partners. Export proceeds of a consignment shipped in 2024 were never realised, and the Directorate of Enforcement alleges that no reasonable steps were taken to realise and repatriate them. During the investigation, documents were seized from the firm's premises and further documents were received from a bank outside India. Mr Devansh Kapoor was the partner in charge of and responsible to the firm for the conduct of its export business throughout; Ms Leela Kapoor, another partner, took no part in the business but personally instructed the overseas buyer to withhold payment. An Adjudicating Authority, who is a Deputy Director of Enforcement, passes an order imposing a penalty, a copy of which is received by the firm on 21 July 2026.

readLink.label: Read: Enforcement, compounding and the appellate ladder →

questions.stem: As to liability for the contravention under section 42 of FEMA 1999:

options.text: Section 42 has no application, because a firm is not a company
options.explanation: The Explanation to s. 42 defines 'company' to mean any body corporate and to include a firm or other association of individuals, and defines 'director' in relation to a firm as a partner.

options.text: The firm and Mr Devansh Kapoor are liable under section 42(1) as the partner in charge of and responsible for the conduct of the business, subject to his defence of no knowledge or due diligence; and Ms Leela Kapoor is separately liable under section 42(2) on the ground of her consent or connivance
options.explanation: Correct. Limb (1) catches the person by office, with the statutory defence; limb (2) operates independently on proof of consent, connivance or neglect, and reaches a partner who was never in charge of the business.

options.text: Only the firm is liable, no partner being liable in the absence of a specific provision
options.explanation: Section 42 exists precisely to fix personal liability alongside that of the entity, and the Explanation brings partners within it.

options.text: All four partners are automatically liable, no defence being available to any of them
options.explanation: Sub-section (1) requires the person to have been in charge of and responsible for the conduct of the business and allows a defence; sub-section (2) requires consent, connivance or neglect to be established. Partners who satisfy neither test are not liable.

questions.stem: The firm decides to appeal against the order. Without seeking condonation of delay, the last date for filing the appeal is:
questions.sourceRef: FEMA 1999, s. 17 — 45 days from the date of receipt of a copy of the order

options.text: 20 August 2026
options.explanation: That is 30 days from receipt. No 30-day appeal period exists under FEMA.

options.text: 19 September 2026
options.explanation: That is 60 days from receipt. Sixty days is the window for an appeal to the High Court under s. 35, not for the first appeal.

options.text: 21 October 2026
options.explanation: That is three calendar months. The section speaks of forty-five days, counted day by day.

options.text: 4 September 2026
options.explanation: Correct. Forty-five days from 21 July 2026 ends on 4 September 2026. The appellate authority may entertain a later appeal on sufficient cause, but that is condonation, which the question excludes.

questions.stem: The appeal referred to above lies to:

options.text: The Special Director (Appeals), the order having been passed by an Adjudicating Authority who is a Deputy Director of Enforcement
options.explanation: Correct. Section 17 routes appeals from orders of an Adjudicating Authority who is an Assistant Director or a Deputy Director of Enforcement to the Special Director (Appeals). Orders of Adjudicating Authorities above that rank go straight to the Appellate Tribunal under s. 19.

options.text: The Appellate Tribunal directly, since all appeals from an Adjudicating Authority lie to it
options.explanation: That is true only of orders passed by an Adjudicating Authority above the rank of Deputy Director. The rank of the officer determines the forum.

options.text: The High Court, an appeal on the merits lying directly from any adjudication order
options.explanation: The High Court's jurisdiction under s. 35 arises only against a decision or order of the Appellate Tribunal, and only on a question of law.

options.text: The Reserve Bank of India, which supervises the Directorate of Enforcement
options.explanation: The Reserve Bank has no appellate role in adjudication, and it does not supervise the Directorate of Enforcement.

questions.stem: As to the documents seized from the firm's premises and those received from the bank outside India, section 39 of FEMA 1999 provides that:

options.text: Such documents are inadmissible unless the person who wrote or signed them is produced as a witness
options.explanation: Section 39 does the opposite: it dispenses with such proof by raising a presumption about handwriting, execution and attestation.

options.text: Documents received from outside India may not be relied on at all in proceedings under the Act
options.explanation: They are expressly covered — the section names documents received from any place outside India in the course of an investigation.

options.text: The court or the Adjudicating Authority shall presume, unless the contrary is proved, the truth of the contents of the documents and that the signature and other handwritten parts are in the handwriting of the person they purport to be, and that a document executed or attested was so executed or attested
options.explanation: Correct. Section 39 raises a rebuttable presumption of both content and authorship, extending to documents produced or furnished, documents seized, and documents received from outside India during an investigation.

options.text: The presumption raised is conclusive and cannot be rebutted by the person proceeded against
options.explanation: The words 'unless the contrary is proved' make the presumption rebuttable. FEMA did not restore FERA's reverse onus on guilt.
